findings.body: The equality lookup misses the blocked entry, so the new user validation accepts an email address that should be blocked. Domain names are case-insensitive, and this path does not normalize the submitted value before querying.
findings.failure_mode: Blocked-email enforcement can be bypassed by changing the casing of the domain portion of an address.
findings.impact: The equality lookup misses the blocked entry, so the new user validation accepts an email address that should be blocked. Domain names are case-insensitive, and this path does not normalize the submitted value before querying.
findings.root_cause: Blocked-email matching compares raw, case-sensitive email strings rather than canonical email identities.
findings.suggested_fix: Canonicalize blocked-email values on write and canonicalize the lookup value using the application's email normalization (for example, `Email.downcase`) before the equality query; add coverage for mixed-case domains.
findings.title: Normalize email before checking the blocked-email table
findings.trigger: A blocked entry is stored as `person@example.com`, and a signup submits the same mailbox with a differently cased domain such as `person@EXAMPLE.COM`.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 12 verbatim shows `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization. Repository context confirms `Email.downcase` exists and is used elsewhere (e.g., `change_email`, `find_by_username_or_email`), but not here. Domain names are case-insensitive per RFC, so `person@EXAMPLE.COM` bypasses a block on `person@example.com`. Realistic trigger with security impact.

findings.body: Both requests can save the same incremented value, losing one or more matches and making `match_count` inaccurate under concurrent attempts.
findings.failure_mode: Concurrent validations overwrite each other's telemetry updates.
findings.impact: Both requests can save the same incremented value, losing one or more matches and making `match_count` inaccurate under concurrent attempts.
findings.root_cause: The read-modify-write update of `match_count` has no atomicity or row lock.
findings.suggested_fix: Perform the increment and timestamp update with an atomic SQL update (or lock the row in a transaction) rather than incrementing an in-memory record and saving it.
findings.title: Make blocked-email match counters atomic
findings.trigger: Two signup validations for the same blocked email run concurrently and both load the record before either saves its increment.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 14 shows `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` at line 16 with no lock or atomic update. Two concurrent requests loading the same record before either saves will both increment from the same base value, losing one count. Classic read-modify-write race condition with clear telemetry impact.

raw_findings.body: Those locale files do not define the newly referenced `user.email.blocked` key, causing users to receive a missing-translation marker or an English fallback instead of a localized validation error.
raw_findings.failure_mode: The blocked-email validation message is incomplete for supported locales.
raw_findings.impact: Those locale files do not define the newly referenced `user.email.blocked` key, causing users to receive a missing-translation marker or an English fallback instead of a localized validation error.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new I18n key was introduced only in the English server locale.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Add `user.email.blocked` translations to the maintained `server.*.yml` locale files, or deliberately use an existing translated key if the message is intended to be identical.

finding.title: Do not permanently cache every server-side email validation failure
finding.trigger: A signup fails with an email error that can later cease to apply, such as a uniqueness error for an account that is subsequently deleted or changes its email, while the create-account controller remains alive.
finding.verifier_reason: The claim is that caching any email error permanently blocks retry. However, the code at line 274-275 only caches when `result.errors.email` is truthy, which is specifically an email validation error from the server. The scenario described (uniqueness error for a deleted account) is speculative and the controller resets `formSubmitted` on failure, allowing resubmission. The impact is ungrounded without evidence that transient errors are cached.
